# User Interface and Tooling

> **Draft chapter map.** Close the book by treating player UI, developer tools, diagnostics, and editors as engine applications built on the same contracts.

## UI Is a Client of the Engine

- Distinguish player-facing UI from editor and diagnostic tools while showing their shared needs.
- Explain why UI needs stable access to input, time, assets, and game-visible state without owning engine internals.

### Player UI and Interaction

- Introduce widgets, layout, and accessibility as game-facing systems; Chapter 5 owns device input and action mapping.
- Connect UI state to the World and game flow without making it renderer-owned state.

#### Composition into the Presented Image

- Explain UI’s render-facing contract and its relationship to resolution and post-processing.
- Discuss menus and loading screens as ordinary lifecycle participants.

## Developer Tools Are Production Systems

- Explain inspection, profiling, asset authoring, and debugging as requirements for a usable engine.
- Connect tools to the observability architecture from Chapter 6.

### Immediate-Mode and Retained Tools

- Compare rapid diagnostic interfaces with persistent editor models.
- Frame the choice around workflow and state ownership rather than fashion.

#### Building an Editor as an Engine Application

- Show how the same public APIs, handles, and plugins can support an editor.
- Explain why this avoids a separate, divergent tool architecture.

## Extensibility, AI, and a Small-Team Workflow

- Connect clear module boundaries, tests, and diagnostics to productive AI-assisted peer programming.
- Explain how architecture makes incremental implementation and review tractable.

### A Durable Engine Is an Understandable Engine

- Revisit the book’s thesis: preserve proven ideas, discard accidental legacy, and choose modern tools deliberately.
- Summarize the recurring questions of ownership, representation, budgets, and evidence.

#### Where the Design Can Evolve

- Identify the interfaces intended to change: plugins, render passes, providers, tools, and content pipelines.
- End with a roadmap mindset rather than a claim of finality.

## Delivery Is Part of the Toolchain

- Treat packaging, platform validation, crash reporting, and update policy as engine-facing concerns.
- Connect reproducible build inputs and release checks to the reliability practices introduced in Chapter 6.

### Shipping Across Platforms

- Explain why a stable engine-facing contract must still be verified against real windowing, driver, input, and deployment environments.
- Frame a release as an evidence-backed artifact rather than merely a compiled executable.
